meta.title: AI-Assisted Decision-Making — Framework Data
meta.source: Notion project 'AI Assisted Decision-Making' (3 linked databases)
meta.structure: factors (framework nodes) <- mechanisms (directional claims) <- studies (coded evidence). Mechanisms are the join: each names one factor and lists supporting and contradicting studies.
meta.id_scheme: Stable slugs held in data/slugs.json, assigned once per Notion page id.
data_notes: Coverage tiers (Well evidenced/Contested/Thin/No evidence yet on factors), status tiers (Above bar/Contested/Below bar on mechanisms), and mechanism direction (Increases/Decreases/No effect/Conditional) were all removed 2026-08-12 at Regina's request: none of these were Notion properties, they were entirely overlay-invented editorial judgement, and she does not want that classification layer on the site. What remains per mechanism is its Notion 'Description' text and its supporting/contradicting studies (n_support/n_contradict, computed from the live relation counts) — mechanisms are ordered by n_support descending everywhere they list.

The Factors database changed shape since the 2026-08-05 export: 'Need for Cognition' was removed as a factor, and 'Task uncertainty' was split out of 'Difficulty' into its own factor. The 2026-08-05 export's f-need-for-cognition overlay entry is now orphaned (harmless, unused).

The Mechanisms database grew from 12 to 17 rows between the 2026-08-05 export and this seed (see AIAssistedDM/2026-08-11-mechanisms-proposal.md, which proposed the 5 additions). This overlay only carries direction/notes for the original 12 — the 5 new mechanisms have no editorial direction or notes yet and will render with those blank until filled in.
'read', 'need_for_cognition', 'own_work', and 'incomplete' are not Notion properties on any database — they only exist in this overlay file, keyed by study id, seeded once from the 2026-08-05 export.

components.label: Human
components.note: What the decision-maker brings. Largely fixed for a given deployment.

components.label: Task
components.note: What the decision is like. Inherited from the domain.

components.label: AI Ecosystem
components.note: What can actually be changed at design time. All three factors here are levers.

factors.definition: How good the AI is — both in absolute terms and, more importantly, relative to the human it is advising. Complementary team performance depends on the second, not the first.
factors.sub_factors: AI accuracy · accuracy relative to the human · shape and predictability of the error boundary ·  complementary expertise
factors.gap_note: BIGGEST CODING GAP IN THE BASE. 24 of 35 studies report absolute accuracy but leave accuracy-relative-to-human unresolved, even though Bansal's central finding is about the relative quantity.

factors.definition: How the AI is presented and when — everything about the interaction other than the explanation itself. The most directly designable factor, and the one where the evidence most openly disagrees.
factors.sub_factors: Interaction protocol and timing · confidence display · advice stance  · interaction modality
factors.gap_note: Protocol is genuinely contested 2-2: Green and Buçinca favour human-first, Cabitza found AI-first produced HIGHER accuracy. Embodiment is an empty node — your IROS 2026 submission is the evidence. Confidence display may deserve promotion to its own factor: it calibrated reliance where explanations did not.

factors.definition: Whether the AI explains itself, and how. The most studied intervention in the field and the one with the most contradictory results.
factors.sub_factors: Explanation presence · explanation type · explanation quality and faithfulness  · explanation cognitive load
factors.gap_note: Densest node in the framework: 7 mechanisms. Explanation QUALITY rests on one study and is absent from Fig. 2.1 entirely. The substitutive/generative distinction is coded from summaries rather than source papers — re-code blind before publishing it.

factors.definition: How many AI advisors speak to the same decision, and how far they agree with one another. Extra advisors add value only when their errors are independent, so returns saturate almost immediately; and agreement among them is read as social consensus rather than as evidence, which makes the effect of consensus non-monotonic in how far the advisors diverge.
factors.sub_factors: Advisor count · agreement configuration among advisors

factors.definition: What the decision-maker already knows — about the task, about AI in general, and about this particular system. Largely fixed for a given deployment: in healthcare the decision-makers are clinicians, and you cannot change that.
factors.sub_factors: Task expertise  · AI expertise / AI literacy · AI system usage (familiarity with this specific system over time)
factors.gap_note: Task expertise is well covered. AI literacy has one data point (Leichtmann: no effect). Longitudinal system usage has NONE — every study in the base is a first-encounter study, flagged in CAT §2.2.1.

factors.definition: Whether the decision is made by one person or several, and how they are structured. Almost the entire literature assumes a single decision-maker facing a single AI.
factors.sub_factors: Individual vs group · group size · group decision mode  · leadership and hierarchy
factors.gap_note: One coded study (Chiang 2023). YOUR CHI 2025 paper is a second and would move this above the bar immediately. This is one of your four thesis contributions — the thinness here is the argument for it.

factors.definition: How hard the decision is: cognitive demand, complexity, and how much work it takes to reach an answer unaided. Determines how expensive it is for the human to work the problem independently rather than defer. Kept separate from Task uncertainty, which is about whether the answer can be verified at all rather than how much effort verifying costs.
factors.gap_note: Difficulty itself is well covered. Outcome uncertainty rests on a single study and is absent from Fig. 2.1 — add it as a named sub-factor.

factors.definition: What it costs to be wrong. Raises the value of getting the decision right, and appears to lower how much people say they trust the AI — though not necessarily how much they actually defer to it.
factors.gap_note: All the evidence is on SELF-REPORTED trust. No study in the base tests whether higher stakes change behavioural reliance. That dissociation is worth a study of its own.

factors.definition: Whether the decision is made under time pressure or in a stress-inducing environment. Compresses the time available to verify, which is exactly the resource that catching a wrong AI requires.
factors.gap_note: One coded study. Rastogi 2022 (Deciding Fast and Slow) is almost certainly a second but has never been coded — code it and this moves above the bar. Nothing at all on stress that is not time pressure.

factors.definition: Whether the correct answer exists at the moment of the decision or only later. Diagnostic tasks ask the human to identify a present state, which can in principle be checked against the evidence in front of them; prognostic tasks ask for a forecast, where no amount of scrutiny can verify the AI before the fact. Distinct from difficulty: a prognostic task can be easy and a diagnostic one hard.

mechanisms.claim: The effect of explanations on decision quality is conditional, not a main effect, and is often null or negative
mechanisms.description:
Asked unconditionally, do explanations help, this literature answers no. Asked conditionally, specifying model performance, task difficulty, risk and explanation form, it answers yes under stated conditions and no otherwise. The row is marked contested by design, because the contest is the finding: the unconditional question is malformed, which is itself the argument for a factor-conditioned framework.

On the negative side, Alufaisan and colleagues ran the three-arm design the field mostly omits, with a no-AI control, an AI-only arm and an AI-plus-explanation arm, and found the AI itself carried the benefit while explanations added nothing. Their methodological point is the most reusable result here: without the AI-only arm, the significant advantage of explanation over an unassisted baseline would have licensed exactly the wrong conclusion. De Brito Duarte and colleagues found the effect of explanation on trust jointly conditional on system performance and risk level, and only feature importance moved anything, with counterfactuals indistinguishable from no explanation for lay users.

On the positive side, Vasconcelos and colleagues obtain clear benefits in hard tasks and with salient explanations, and Leichtmann and colleagues find explanations improving accuracy on precisely the items where the classifier erred, while lowering trust in a way they read as better calibration.

Read together with the checkability and engagement-cost mechanisms, the conditions under which explanations help are becoming specifiable rather than mysterious.
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Alufaisan (three-arm design with a no-AI control — 'the why information provided in explainable AI may not enhance user decision-making'), de Brito Duarte (OWN MSc — explanation effect on trust is jointly conditional on system performance and risk level), Wang and Yin (four XAI methods on two task types — most 'not as helpful as expected and even harmful at times'). CONTESTED BY DESIGN: Vasconcelos and Gajos both produce clear positive effects under specified conditions. The right reading is not that explanations do nothing but that the unconditional question 'do explanations help?' is malformed — which is itself the argument for a factor-conditioned framework.

mechanisms.claim: Calibrated reliance requires knowing when the AI fails, which case-level confidence supports and explanations do not
mechanisms.description:
Knowing that a model is 80% accurate tells the decision-maker nothing about the case in front of them. What supports selective reliance is a usable model of the error boundary, meaning where in the input space the system fails, and the properties of that boundary matter as much as the accuracy figure attached to it.

The two Bansal 2019 papers establish both halves. Mental model quality mediates the relationship between AI accuracy and team performance, and boundaries that are less parsimonious, higher-dimensional or stochastic are learned poorly or not at all: a two-sided stochastic boundary was never learned, with the proportion of optimal choices flat near 50% across rounds. The corollary is that an update improving accuracy can reduce team performance by invalidating the boundary the human has already learned.

Case-level confidence is the intervention that works. Zhang, Liao and Bellamy show reliance tracking model confidence when the score is displayed and flat across confidence bins when it is not, and Bansal 2021 found a confidence display alone achieved complementarity that no explanation condition improved upon, with a quarter of participants adopting explicit personal confidence thresholds. Reverberi and colleagues show experts doing this natively, weighting each case by their own confidence and their reading of the AI's.

The boundary condition is that a good mental model only pays off where the human can act on it. Zhang, Liao and Bellamy calibrated trust successfully and gained no accuracy, because the model was uncertain exactly where the humans were also wrong.

The contradicting evidence is substantial and should not be discounted. Green and Chen found participants unable to estimate model accuracy at all across six conditions, Chiang and colleagues found understanding of the model close to nil in both individuals and groups, and Bussone and colleagues found displayed confidence had almost no effect on reliance, with several clinicians unable to say what the percentage meant.
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Bansal 2019a (error boundary mediates AI accuracy to team performance), Bansal 2019b (updates that improve the model HURT the team by invalidating the learned failure pattern), Zhang 2020 (case-level confidence calibrates, global accuracy cannot), Bansal 2021 (users built mental models from confidence and used it whether or not explanations were shown), Reverberi (experts weight-integrate: OR 3.48 correct vs 1.85 incorrect, with NO explanation), Kiani (model performance in isolation does not transfer; benefit confined to an experience band), Leichtmann (case-level explanation helped, general education about the AI did not). LARGEST AND MOST INDEPENDENT SUPPORT SET IN THE BASE. CONTRADICTION: Bussone found system confidence had only a slight effect — with domain experts, where the mental model may already exist.

mechanisms.claim: Explanations help only when the user can check them against the case
mechanisms.description:
What determines whether an explanation improves a decision is not how much it explains but whether the user can hold it against the evidence and see a mismatch. Explanations that are inspectable at a glance, such as similar cases shown as images or a highlight drawn on the artefact itself, let people form their own reading first and make the model's errors visible. Explanations that must be reasoned about in the abstract, such as feature weights, counterfactuals or fluent prose, are visually or rhetorically dominant, suppress the user's own reading of the case, and are accepted without being checked.

Fluency makes this worse rather than better: the most conversational interface in the base produced the worst self-reliance and the worst objective understanding at the same time. The mechanism is distinct from explanation quality, since a faithful explanation in an uncheckable form still displaces judgement, and from explanation stance, since it concerns the format of what is shown rather than whether a conclusion is withheld.

Chen and colleagues provide the cleanest within-study contrast, with example-based explanations achieving complementarity on both tasks while feature-based explanations achieved none and actively hurt when the AI was wrong. The contradicting case is Cabitza and colleagues on knee MRI, where saliency maps, an inspectable form, were clearly detrimental under human-first protocols.

mechanisms.claim: People check the AI only when checking is cheaper than being wrong, so difficulty, time and explanation load set over-reliance
mechanisms.description:
Accepting the AI is a strategy with a cost of nearly zero, and verifying it is a strategy with a cost set by the task, the time available and the legibility of the explanation. People choose between them rationally, so over-reliance rises whenever verification becomes expensive relative to the penalty for error, and falls when an intervention makes verification cheap or makes error costly.

This reframes a decade of null findings on explanations as a sampling problem. Vasconcelos and colleagues manipulate both sides of the trade across five studies and reproduce the field's standard null in easy and medium tasks while overturning it in hard ones; a maximally salient explanation drove over-reliance to zero, and raising the monetary penalty for error reduced it independently.

The time studies supply the same logic from the other direction. Rastogi and colleagues show that buying more time buys more adjustment away from the anchor, and Swaroop and colleagues show over-reliance rising from 0.41 to 0.59 when time pressure is imposed on an AI-first protocol. Westphal and colleagues provide the only measured mediator in the base, tracing the harm of explanations through increased perceived task complexity.

The standing contradiction is Green and Chen, who varied presentation across six conditions, effectively varying cost, and still found reliance failing to track model performance, which suggests cost is not the whole story.
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Vasconcelos (cost-benefit framework, 5 studies N=731, manipulates both cost and benefit), Westphal (only MEASURED mediator in the base — explanation harm ran through increased perceived task complexity), Rastogi (time as the scarce resource), Time-pressure 2024 (pressure raises over-reliance while holding accuracy), Buçinca 2021 (people default to heuristics rather than per-case analysis because analysis is costly). FOUR INDEPENDENT LABS converging from three theories. CONTRADICTION: Green and Chen varied presentation across six conditions — effectively varying cost — and reliance still did not track performance, suggesting cost is not the whole story.

mechanisms.claim: Cutting over-reliance usually raises under-reliance, so accuracy does not move
mechanisms.description: Most interventions that make people less willing to accept the AI make them less willing to accept it when it is right as well as when it is wrong. The two movements cancel, which is why so many designs succeed on one reliance measure and vanish on decision quality. A reported reduction in over-reliance is therefore uninformative unless the corresponding under-reliance figure is given alongside it.

mechanisms.claim: Expertise decides who benefits from AI support, but not in a fixed direction
mechanisms.description:
There is no stable law relating expertise to reliance in this evidence base, and claims of the form novices over-rely while experts resist are not supported. The same class of support raises novices to expert level in one clinical study and reaches only the experienced in another; experts are more discriminating in some settings and measurably less so in others. Measured knowledge, as opposed to professional role, frequently predicts nothing at all.

The two Cabitza studies make the point most sharply by pointing in opposite directions with comparable populations: in one, AI support closed the gap between novices and experts, while in another residents outperformed specialists unaided, no resident improved with support, and automation bias among residents was two and a half times that of specialists. Sivaraman and colleagues found their four behaviour patterns were not explained by seniority at all, and Leichtmann and colleagues found neither domain knowledge nor AI knowledge predicted performance.

What does appear to travel is that the fit between the support and the user's existing process matters more than the user's level, which is why Calisto and colleagues could improve novice accuracy by changing only the register in which the same recommendation was delivered.

mechanisms.claim: A coherent-looking explanation substitutes for verification, so people stop checking
mechanisms.description:
An explanation that looks sound is taken as evidence that the recommendation is sound, and the check that would have caught the error is never performed. The harm arrives through the form of the explanation looking right rather than through the effort it demands, which distinguishes this mechanism from the engagement-cost one: here the explanation is cheap to read and that is precisely the problem.

Cabitza and colleagues 2024 give the sharpest demonstration and name it the XAI halo effect. Participants solving logic puzzles with verifiable answers received correct advice accompanied by either a relevant or an irrelevant explanation, and did significantly worse with the irrelevant one, a large effect. They could have checked the advice against the puzzle directly and did not.

The same pattern appears without any manipulation of faithfulness. Bansal and colleagues 2021 found explanations raised acceptance whether the recommendation was right or wrong, so gains and losses cancelled. Cabitza and colleagues on medical protocols found the increase in trust from explanations occurred irrespective of whether the advice was correct. He and colleagues describe the interactive version as an illusion of explanatory depth, with perceived understanding, perceived utility and trust all rising while over-reliance did not fall.

The most striking case removes the authority entirely: in Cabitza and colleagues 2025 the system asserted nothing and presented arguments for both diagnoses, and a fifth of participants were still argued out of correct answers by the map supporting the wrong one. Persuasiveness alone is sufficient; no deference to machine authority is required.

The design implication the authors draw is to withhold explanations rather than risk poor ones.
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Cabitza 2024 Harmful (the 'XAI HALO EFFECT' — accurate advice plus misleading explanation, participants 'did not verify the correctness of the advice'), Bussone (fuller explanation raised trust AND produced over-reliance), Bansal 2021 ('explanations increased reliance on recommendations even when the AI was incorrect'), He 2025 conversational XAI (understanding and trust both rose while over-reliance was unchanged). THE MECHANISM IS FORM, NOT COST: harm arrives through the explanation looking right, independent of how much effort it demands. Sharpest evidence that an explanation can satisfy a transparency requirement while degrading oversight. CONTRADICTION: Leichtmann found attribution plus example-based explanations improved outcomes and produced better-calibrated trust.

mechanisms.claim: Reliance is not one quantity: over-reliance, under-reliance and stated trust move independently
mechanisms.description:
This is a measurement mechanism, and it constrains how every other row in this table may be read. An intervention can improve one component of reliance while leaving the failure mode of interest untouched, and a study reporting only agreement rates or only self-reported trust cannot distinguish the two.

Schemmer and colleagues show the decomposition doing real work: explanations moved relative positive AI reliance significantly while relative positive self-reliance did not move at all, so uptake of good advice improved and resistance to bad advice did not. He and colleagues show the reverse asymmetry, with self-reliance collapsing across every interactive interface while AI reliance barely improved. Salimzadeh and colleagues show a rise in one component that looks like improvement and is not, since participants simply under-relied on easy tasks and over-relied on hard ones.

Two further studies attack the measures themselves. Bucinca and colleagues 2020 demonstrate that proxy tasks do not generalise to real decision tasks and that subjective measures do not predict objective performance, in a double dissociation. Sivaraman and colleagues show that binary agreement is mis-specified for experts, who accepted parts of a recommendation, adjusted its dosage or shifted its timing, with negotiation the largest of four behaviour patterns and full acceptance or rejection the rarest.

The practical rule that follows: any mechanism whose only evidence is trust or preference stands on weaker ground than one evidenced behaviourally, and any reported change in over-reliance should be read alongside the corresponding under-reliance figure.
mechanisms.notes: STRUCTURAL / MEASUREMENT MECHANISM — it constrains how every other row in this table may be read. MERGED FROM: Schemmer (explanations moved RAIR significantly, RSR not at all — uptake of good advice improved, resistance to bad advice did not), Sivaraman (expert reliance is partial and component-wise — 'ignore, trust, or NEGOTIATE' — so binary agreement measures are mis-specified), Buçinca 2020 (proxy tasks do not generalise to real decision tasks and subjective measures do not predict objective performance), He 2025 (understanding and trust rose while over-reliance held constant), Salimzadeh (reliance moved with uncertainty while trust did not move at all). FIVE STUDIES, FOUR INDEPENDENT GROUPS. Practical rule: any mechanism in this table whose only evidence is trust or preference is on weaker ground than one evidenced behaviourally.

mechanisms.claim: AI systems that promote reflection reduce over-reliance
mechanisms.description:
Reflective designs withhold the recommendation, or add a layer that argues with it, and in every study in the base that measured over-reliance under such a design, over-reliance fell. The effect is more consistent than the effect of explanations, which the explanation-presence rows record as conditional and frequently null.

Ma and colleagues give the largest reduction with the cleanest control on effort: over-reliance fell from 0.65 to 0.47, p < .001, under Deliberative AI against conventional XAI, while workload showed no significant differences in mental demand, effort or perceived complexity across the three conditions. The reduction therefore cannot be attributed to raised cognitive load alone, which distinguishes it from the friction-based interventions recorded elsewhere in this table.

Li and colleagues reproduce it with a wholly static intervention: four reflection questions derived from Pennycook's dual-process model cut over-reliance from 0.58 to 0.34, p < .05, and raised accuracy from 0.817 to 0.881, p < .05, with under-reliance flat at 0.05 against 0.04. One comparison the authors step past belongs on this row: the plain AI arm without explanations sat at 0.33, so the prompts repaired damage the SHAP plots had done rather than pushing over-reliance below a no-explanation baseline.

Tian and colleagues find it again with a conversational critic of the participant's own argument, over-reliance 0.67 to 0.543, p = .035, d = -0.365. Chiang and colleagues find it for an interactive devil's advocate, though only marginally, F(1,91) = 3.554, p = 0.063. Reicherts and colleagues do not measure over-reliance directly but report the closest available proxy, with 45.00% of trades matching the AI's recommendations under RecommendAI against 23.08% of trades departing from the participant's own written rationale under ExtendAI.

Two scope conditions belong on this row.

First, reducing over-reliance is not the same as improving decisions, and this claim should not be read as asserting it. Ma and Li both convert the reduction into accuracy gains with under-reliance unmoved. Tian does not: under-reliance rose from 0.202 to 0.281, p = .019, d = 0.409, and balanced accuracy did not differ across any treatment, which is the see-saw recorded elsewhere. The sharpest open question the base can now pose is what separates the first two from the third, and the candidate distinction is whether the reflection is directed at the AI's reasoning or at the decision-maker's own.

Second, cognitive forcing functions are deliberately excluded. Delay, on-request and partial explanations raise the cost of accepting the AI without withholding its answer, and under the evidence base's Advice stance coding they are Directive rather than Reflective. Bucinca 2021, de Jong 2025 and Gajos 2022 therefore do not support this row even though they also reduce over-reliance. Folding them in would make the claim unfalsifiable by letting every friction-based design count as reflection.

mechanisms.claim: Withholding the AI's conclusion is what produces learning; handing over a rationale does not
mechanisms.description:
When a recommendation is present the decision-maker can reach an answer without processing the explanation, and does. Remove the recommendation while keeping the same explanatory content and the explanation becomes the only route to an answer, so it must be processed, and processing it leaves knowledge behind. The claim is about skill acquisition specifically: performance and learning are separable outcomes that interface design can trade against each other.

Gajos and Mamykina isolate this as cleanly as anything in the base, holding explanation content identical across three experiments and finding learning only in the condition where the conclusion was withheld. The update protocol, which reduces over-reliance, produced no learning at all.

The claim has been deliberately narrowed. It previously also asserted a reduction in over-reliance, which the evidence no longer supports as part of the same mechanism: Bucinca and colleagues 2025 obtained a clear learning gain from contrastive explanations while over-reliance was unchanged, and participants still fell to roughly half their unaided accuracy on the items the AI got wrong. Reduced over-reliance belongs to the engagement-cost mechanism instead.

Two caveats carry over. The effect is gated by cognitive load, and it is concentrated in one research community, with several of the supporting studies coming from the same two labs. Gajos and Mamykina also found the learning gain was larger for participants already high in Need for Cognition, so deploying it may widen a gap rather than close one.
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Gajos and Mamykina (CLEANEST EXPERIMENT IN THE BASE — three conditions, learning gains ONLY where the conclusion was withheld, identical explanatory content), Chen/Liao (within-study: feature-based increased over-reliance, example-based achieved complementarity), Cabitza pro-hoc ('Frictional AI'), Cabitza judicial (oracular to judicial), Ma (procedural deliberation), Buçinca 2021 (cognitive forcing), Buçinca 2025 (contrastive knowledge-gap alignment). TWO CAVEATS THAT MUST BE STATED: (1) GATED BY COGNITIVE LOAD — the two highest-load cases came out flat on over-reliance; (2) SEVERE LAB CONCENTRATION — four of seven are Gajos/Buçinca at Harvard, two are Cabitza/Natali. CONTRADICTION: Cabitza Rams found AI-first produced HIGHER diagnostic accuracy than human-first, with real radiologists on hard cases.

mechanisms.claim: Reflective support shifts the interpretive burden onto the user, so it helps the capable and can harm the rest
mechanisms.description:
Removing the recommendation removes the shortcut. Whoever cannot perform the interpretation the recommendation used to spare them is left worse off than they would have been with a directive system, so the benefit of reflective design is conditional on the user's capacity to supply what the system withholds.

Cabitza and colleagues 2025 give the strongest and most uncomfortable version. Judicial AI, which issues no recommendation and instead presents one activation map supporting the presence of a fracture and one supporting its absence, produced a large significant benefit for more experienced clinicians, Glass's Delta 0.99, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.47, p = .045. For less experienced clinicians the point estimate was negative, Delta -0.148, 95% CI -0.45 to 0.161, and non-inferiority to unaided diagnosis could not be established, Z = 1.2491, p = .1058. The authors name this as the study's main caution in their own terms: a protocol that demands interpretation may not be safe for those least equipped to interpret.

Danry and colleagues show the same conditionality located in the case rather than the person. Socratic questioning beat causal explanation where independent scrutiny was needed, on logically invalid statements, 62.5 against 55.0, p = .009, and lost its advantage where it was not, on valid statements, 74.7 against 78.2, p = .126. A question is worth more than an answer only when accepting the answer would have been a mistake.

Li and colleagues report that both moderators of their reflection effect were individual capacities rather than states, so who benefited was largely determined before the intervention began. Tian and colleagues found no learning effect for any treatment and no improvement on minority-label cases for any form of assistance, so the reflective arms did not lift the harder cases for a general population.

This row is a scope condition on the reflection claims rather than a contradiction of them, and it sits deliberately against the expertise row. That row records that there is no stable direction relating expertise to reliance across the base as a whole. Here the direction is consistent, because this class of design mechanically transfers interpretive work to the user instead of leaving the division of labour for the participant to negotiate.

mechanisms.claim: Interventions that reduce over-reliance by imposing effort are rated worse by the people they protect
mechanisms.description:
Designs that protect people from the AI's errors by making them do more cognitive work are experienced as worse systems.

The scope condition matters and keeps the claim narrow. It applies to interventions that work by raising the cost of accepting the AI, such as cognitive forcing functions or forced deliberation. It does not apply to interventions that reduce over-reliance by making verification cheaper, which people willingly pay for: participants in Vasconcelos and colleagues assigned the highest subjective utility to precisely the explanation formats that produced the largest reductions in over-reliance.

Bucinca and colleagues supply the direct evidence, correlating each participant's own trust against their own performance on the items where the AI erred. Ma and colleagues sharpen it: deliberation was trusted and liked significantly less despite no measurable increase in workload, so the aversion is to having to defend one's own view rather than to effort as such.

mechanisms.claim: Forcing an independent judgement first can backfire, entrenching a wrong prior or triggering rejection of correct advice
mechanisms.description:
Human-first protocols are widely recommended on the grounds that committing to a judgement before seeing the AI protects against anchoring. This mechanism records the counter-evidence: committing first can entrench a wrong prior through conservatism bias, and seeing the AI as a challenge to a position already taken can trigger rejection of correct advice.

Cabitza and colleagues found AI-first protocols significantly more accurate than human-first in both of their studies, with a large effect in the ECG study, and more accurate than both the unaided readers and the AI alone. The authors expected the opposite and name the candidate mechanisms themselves: conservatism bias and belief perseverance when the AI opposes a recorded judgement, against a replacement effect under AI-first in which the AI substitutes for the clinician's initial intuition and frees them to reason more deliberately.

Swaroop and colleagues add a qualified second case: under time pressure an AI-before protocol was faster than AI-after at no cost in accuracy, though it carried higher over-reliance, so the advantage is on the accuracy-time trade-off rather than on accuracy alone.

This mechanism stands in direct tension with the withheld-conclusion mechanism, and the tension is real rather than a coding artefact. It is also the only place in the base where the disagreement is between two studies by the same group, since Cabitza and colleagues 2025 found a human-first judicial protocol helping experienced clinicians on complex cases. The distinguishing variable may be whether the AI issues a verdict at all.
mechanisms.notes: FROM: Cabitza Rams — AI-FIRST protocols were associated with HIGHER diagnostic accuracy than human-first, with 12 specialist radiologists on knee MRI and 44 ECG readers. The authors name the mechanisms: ALGORITHMIC AVERSION (seeing the AI first can trigger rejection of correct advice) and CONSERVATISM BIAS (committing first can entrench a wrong prior). THIS IS THE DIRECT COUNTERWEIGHT to the withheld-conclusion mechanism, and it is the only study in the base run with real domain experts on genuinely hard clinical cases. Below bar on one study, but it is a high-quality one and the disagreement is real rather than a coding artefact — do not resolve it prematurely.

mechanisms.claim: When verification is impossible rather than merely expensive, reliance rises and no explanation design fixes it
mechanisms.description:
This mechanism is critically distinct from the engagement-cost one: lowering the price of checking does nothing when checking is not possible. Where the ground truth is not available at decision time, where the outcome is genuinely uncertain, or where the human simply lacks the knowledge the case requires, there is no basis on which to override, and reliance rises by default.

Salimzadeh and colleagues manipulate uncertainty directly and find participants leaning harder on the AI precisely where they were least able to distinguish good advice from bad. Green and Chen produce the strongest version across six presentation conditions: participants could evaluate neither their own accuracy nor the model's in any of them, an empty cycle of oversight.

Bucinca and colleagues 2025 supply the blunt statement of the consequence. Across every condition of their study, including the contrastive explanations that produced real learning gains, accuracy on the items the AI got wrong fell to 0.14 against 0.29 unaided. Assistance roughly halved unaided performance on exactly the cases where the model failed, and no explanation design in that study altered it.

This is the strongest argument in the base against assuming that human oversight, as required by EU AI Act Article 14 and comparable provisions, is protective in prognostic or high-uncertainty deployments. Oversight presupposes a capacity to verify that the task itself may not afford.
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Salimzadeh ('individuals may lack sufficient capability to verify the correctness of AI advice' under uncertainty), Green and Chen (participants could evaluate neither their own nor the model's accuracy across all six treatments — the 'empty cycle of oversight'), Wang and Yin (explanations convey reasoning but not model uncertainty, leaving no basis for selective override). CRITICALLY DISTINCT FROM THE COST MECHANISM: lowering the price of checking does nothing when checking is not possible. This is the strongest argument in the base against assuming EU AI Act Article 14 human oversight is protective in prognostic or high-uncertainty deployments.

mechanisms.claim: Raising the stakes makes people more discriminating about AI advice, and can reduce trust
mechanisms.description:
Stakes how selectively people take AI advice. Three studies raise the stakes three different ways: a monetary bonus, an in-game consequence, and a change of domain. What changes when stakes are high is the response to advice that should be resisted, or that challenges the decision-maker, not the response to advice that confirms them.

Vasconcelos and colleagues supply the incentive version and the cleanest test in the base. Study 4 was pre-registered, ran the hard maze task only, and blocked the monetary bonus within subjects at 0.01 USD against 0.50 USD per correct maze, holding the task, the AI and the explanation constant so that only the payoff differed. Over-reliance, defined as acceptance of incorrect AI predictions, was lower under the larger bonus (0.93, 95% CI 0.414 to 1.46). This is the benefit half of their cost-benefit framework: over-reliance is treated as a strategic choice, so raising the return on being right buys more verification. They draw a methodological consequence worth carrying: crowdsourced studies that pay a performance bonus may not replicate those that do not.

Li and colleagues supply the selectivity directly. Where the assistant confirmed the participant's initial choice, task risk made no difference to adoption (beta = 0.377, p = 0.415). Where it contradicted them, adoption was significantly higher in the high-risk ETF task than in the low-risk dating task (beta = 0.843, p < 0.001). In the authors' words, task risk selectively amplifies the influence of contradictory, rather than confirmatory, AI advice.

mechanisms.claim: A human partner amplifies whatever the interface affords rather than adding a fixed pull toward the AI
mechanisms.description:
Partnership multiplies whatever the interface already encourages, so the same manipulation that produces the most careful decision-makers in a study produces the most careless ones when the interface gives them nothing to work with.

de Brito Duarte and colleagues supply the interaction directly. Over-reliance showed a main effect of explanations, F(1,55) = 9.523, p = 0.004, eta-squared 0.192, and an interaction with team composition, F(1,55) = 6.098, p = 0.018, eta-squared 0.132, with no main effect of team composition at all, F = 0.006, p = 0.94. Within the group condition over-reliance was 0.82 without explanations and 0.125 with them, and the simple effect of explanations is significant only in the group condition. A pair given a bare recommendation followed a wrong AI in four cases out of five; the same pair given a feature-importance chart followed it in one case out of eight. The absent main effect is the crux of the claim: partnership on its own does nothing in either direction.

Chiang and colleagues 2023 is the bare-interface case. Participants saw a COMPAS label with no confidence and no explanation, so there was nothing to scrutinise together, and groups over-relied more than individuals, 0.53 rising to 0.68, adjusted p = 0.010, with decision accuracy unchanged at 57.8% against 55.3%. Chiang and colleagues 2024 is the same team on the same task with something to argue against, and the interactive devil's advocate targeting the AI recommendation was the only treatment to significantly improve group accuracy, beta = 0.135, p = 0.047.

This row was written to resolve a conflict rather than to report a new finding. Read as a fixed pull toward the AI, group deliberation is contradicted by two of the three real-group studies in the base. Read as amplification, all three agree.

Two things to settle. The existing row stating that group deliberation raises reliance on the AI now rests on Chiang 2023 alone and asserts something different about the same evidence; one of the two rows should go, and the choice is Regina's because the claim is hers. Separately, amplification does not cover Daryanto and colleagues 2026, where a partner cut AI code adoption from 23.1% to roughly 1.3% in both triadic conditions regardless of what the AI offered. That is a level effect rather than an interaction and belongs to a separate accountability claim.

mechanisms.claim: Extra AI advisors add value only through error independence, so returns saturate almost immediately
mechanisms.description:
The value of a second opinion comes from its errors falling on different cases, not from its existence. Advisors drawn from the same system share an error boundary, so the first addition carries most of the available gain and further additions carry almost none.

Tsuchiya and Baba built the control that isolates this. Every advisor was a decision tree drawn from a Rashomon set and calibrated to exactly 70% accuracy, so three advisors agreeing were by construction no more likely to be right than one. Three advisors nonetheless beat one on income prediction, M = .737 against .706, p = .012, and on dating prediction, Mdn = .68 against .64, p = .002. Five beat three on nothing: marginal on dating at p = .064, and recidivism showed no panel-size effect at all, F(2,81) = 2.33, p = .104. The curve flattens after three.

Lu, Wang and Yin supply the null on the outcome that matters. Second opinions presented on every task cut over-reliance, Cohen's d 0.26 to 0.44, and raised under-reliance, d 0.14 to 0.22, with appropriate reliance showing no significant difference. More advice and more time spent bought no better decisions.

Berger and colleagues state the independence argument positively and give it its boundary. Handing human-AI disagreements to a fresh second human, rather than asking the first human to adjudicate the machine, resolved correct AI judgements 71% of the time against 34% under the advisor arrangement, and the hybrid confirmation tree beat AI-as-advisor in all ten datasets, pooling to 4.45 percentage points, 95% HDI 3.73 to 5.27. The boundary condition is explicit and should be read with the claim: independent aggregation only helps where the independent human signal carries information, and all three losses across the sixteen explainable-AI conditions came from deception detection, where unaided human accuracy is 51.1%, essentially chance.

The relationship to the advisor-consensus row is deliberate and neither row is redundant. That row concerns how agreement is read, as social pressure rather than as evidence. This one concerns what agreement is worth, which is nothing when the advisors share an error boundary. They are the perception and the reality of the same display.

mechanisms.claim: A human-AI team beats both members only when the AI is right where the human is wrong
mechanisms.description: Complementarity is a property of the relationship between two error distributions, not of the AI's accuracy. A system weaker than the average human produces a team better than either when its mistakes fall on different cases; a system stronger than the human produces no gain at all when their mistakes coincide. This explains the most common shape of results in the base, where assistance lifts people above their unaided performance but never above the AI alone: the overlap sets the ceiling, and no interface change moves it. The practical implication is that model selection for deployment should be driven by error independence from the intended user, which is almost never what accuracy benchmarks measure.

mechanisms.claim: Advice the decision-maker asked for behaves differently from advice imposed on them
mechanisms.description:
Control over the information flow, rather than the information itself, shapes the reliance profile. In the studies supporting this mechanism the content of the advice is held constant and only the user's authority over it changes: whether a second opinion arrives unbidden or on request, and whether the recommendation can be adjusted or only accepted or rejected. Both manipulations move trust, understanding and compliance while the underlying advice stays the same.

Lu, Wang and Yin show that always-present second opinions cut over-reliance but raised under-reliance, whereas second opinions the participant chose to solicit reduced over-reliance without that penalty, though only a third of participants ever solicited one. Westphal and colleagues show the adjustment side: empowering users to modify the recommendation raised trust, understanding and both intended and actual compliance, while explanation presence in the same three studies did nothing or harmed.

The mechanism has a direct bearing on multi-agent and ensemble settings, which are by construction the always-present condition, and which this mechanism predicts will trade over-reliance for under-reliance rather than improving decisions.
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Lu, Wang and Yin (three pre-registered experiments — ALWAYS-PRESENT second opinions cut over-reliance but RAISED under-reliance, regardless of whether the source was a peer or another AI; SOLICITED second opinions mitigated over-reliance WITHOUT that penalty), Westphal (decision control — empowering users to ADJUST recommendations — raised trust, understanding and compliance, while explanation presence in the same study did the opposite). THE CONTENT IS HELD CONSTANT IN BOTH: what changes is who decides when it arrives and whether it can be altered. Directly relevant to RQ6: a multi-agent setting is by construction the always-present condition, which this mechanism predicts will trade over-reliance for under-reliance.

mechanisms.claim: How the AI speaks changes how much it is believed, with identical content
mechanisms.description:
Nothing about the information changes, only the register in which it is asserted, and reliance changes anyway. The mechanism is social and communicative rather than cognitive, and the optimal register appears to depend on the recipient rather than being a fixed property of good design.

This row previously rested on one study and was flagged as unsettled. It now has four, spanning clinical experts, crowdworkers and two different senses of register, which is the strongest thing that happened to this table in the 2026-08-14 pass.

Calisto and colleagues remain the cleanest case: an imposing tone and a suggestive tone delivering identical breast-cancer diagnostic content produced different diagnoses, with novices more accurate under the assertive register and experts slightly better under the suggestive one. The gain came almost entirely from novices ceasing to overturn correct recommendations, with acceptance of incorrect ones essentially unchanged, at no measurable workload cost and with diagnosis time cut by a quarter.

Li and colleagues supply the strongest control. Four chatbots drew on an identical knowledge base and differed only in social register, and the register that changed behaviour was opinion agreement, which significantly reduced the likelihood of revising a decision under contradicting evidence. Direct praise and self-deprecation, which participants recognised as flattery, moved perceptions and confidence but not decisions. The manipulation that worked was the one nobody detected.

De Brito Duarte and colleagues extend the claim from register to modality: the same TreeSHAP or LORE explanation delivered through a chatbot rather than as static text significantly raised agreement with the recommendation and lowered the rate of declining to commit, with no gain in accuracy, which the authors read as a persuasive rather than an epistemic effect. Munyaka and colleagues supply a fourth variant, source framing: with the partner's advice hard-coded and identical, labelling it human rather than AI raised adoption from 1.44 to 2.10 of five suggestions.

The contradicting case sets the limit. Tsuchiya and Baba varied anthropomorphic presentation of three identical advisors and found perceived usefulness and agency rising without average conformity pressure changing, so presentation moved perception without moving behaviour. Read against the other four, the pattern is that register changes behaviour when it changes the social relation to the advice, and changes only attitudes when it changes the advisor's appearance.

Two housekeeping notes carried forward: the sub-factor was corrected from Confidence display, which described a different construct entirely, and the previously claimed support from Zhang, Lee and Carter was withdrawn because that coded row evidences complementary expertise rather than a language manipulation.
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Calisto (assertive versus suggestive tone delivering IDENTICAL breast-cancer diagnostic content; personalising assertiveness to clinician experience REDUCED MEDICAL ERRORS and raised satisfaction), Zhang, Lee and Carter ('embracing' language INCREASED reliance, 'distancing' language REDUCED it — same information, differently worded). TWO INDEPENDENT STUDIES, DIFFERENT POPULATIONS (clinicians and crowdworkers), SAME CONCLUSION. Mechanism is social and communicative rather than cognitive: nothing about the information changes, only the register in which it is asserted, and the optimal register depends on the recipient's expertise. The most under-theorised family in the literature.

mechanisms.claim: Pooling independent AI-assisted judgements suppresses over-reliance without any deliberation, because over-reliance errors are idiosyncratic
mechanisms.description:
Where the deliberation mechanism concerns people talking to one another, this one concerns people never meeting at all. Several individuals each decide with the AI, their judgements are combined by a rule, and the aggregate is better than any of them. The reason is statistical: the cases on which a given person is talked out of a correct answer are not the same cases for the next person, so uncritical acceptance of a bad recommendation rarely survives a majority. Nothing about the individual's reliance improves; the errors are diluted.

Gu and colleagues demonstrate it in pathology, computing majority votes offline by resampling from 32 individual pathologists' AI-assisted responses. Relative self-reliance rose at every panel size (all p < 0.001) and relative AI reliance rose from three raters upward, so both components of reliance improved together rather than trading off, and precision improved from five raters upward (p < 0.001). The authors name the mechanism as dilution of idiosyncratic over-reliance.

Berger and colleagues generalise it across ten datasets. Replacing the advisory protocol with a hybrid confirmation tree, in which human and AI judge in parallel and disagreements escalate to a second independent human, beat AI-assisted advising by 4.45 accuracy points pooled (95% HDI 3.73 to 5.27) and in every dataset. The comparison against sixteen explainable-AI conditions is the sharper result: restructuring who decides beat every attempt to improve what the decision-maker was shown.

mechanisms.claim: Advice that agrees with the decision-maker's prior is weighted most heavily, so human and AI errors reinforce each other
mechanisms.description:
Whether advice is taken depends less on its content than on whether it matches the judgement the person had already formed. Congruent advice is weighted more heavily and raises confidence; incongruent advice is discounted even when correct. The consequence is the opposite of what assistance is meant to deliver: the cases where the AI could correct a human error are exactly the cases where its advice is congruent with nothing and gets discounted, while the cases where human and machine are wrong together produce the strongest agreement and the highest confidence.

Rosbach and colleagues measured the weighting directly in expert pathologists. Where the AI agreed with the pathologist's own estimate, recorded two weeks earlier, the final answer loaded 0.60 on the AI; where it disagreed, 0.43, with the participant's own prior carrying more weight at 0.47 and confidence falling from 3.87 to 3.24. The model erred on roughly half the patches, so correlated error was not hypothetical.

Li and colleagues manipulate the congruence rather than observing it, and find the same asymmetry from the other side. An assistant that simply echoed the user's stated reasoning significantly reduced the likelihood of revising a decision when the assistant then presented contradicting evidence, while explicit flattery, which participants recognised as strategic, did not. The mechanism the authors propose is confirmation rather than persuasion: agreement acts as social validation that strengthens the anchor the user has already set. Crucially, the manipulation that changed behaviour was the one participants could not detect, and it was invisible on their manipulation check.

Two boundary conditions. Li and colleagues found that raising task stakes increased adoption of contradicting advice specifically, without changing adoption of confirming advice, so the entrenchment is not fixed. And neither study reports decision accuracy, so the claim describes how congruence moves weighting, not how much it costs. This mechanism is distinct from the coherent-explanation one, where the explanation's apparent soundness does the work; here the persuasive property is agreement with the person rather than any property of the reasoning.

mechanisms.claim: Agreement among AI advisors is read as social consensus rather than as evidence, so its effect is non-monotonic in how far they diverge
mechanisms.description:
When several AI advisors speak, people respond to how many of them agree rather than to what that agreement is worth. In both supporting studies the agreement carries no evidential content by construction, and it moves behaviour anyway, which is what identifies the pressure as social rather than informational. The effect is not monotonic in consensus: a single dissenting voice relieves it, and wide disagreement replaces it with confusion.

Tsuchiya and Baba built the decisive control. Every advisor was a decision tree drawn from a Rashomon set and calibrated to exactly 70% accuracy, so three advisors agreeing were no more likely to be right than one. High consensus nonetheless fostered over-reliance, a single dissenter reduced the pressure to conform, and wide disagreement produced overload that undermined appropriate reliance. Accuracy rose from one advisor to three (.706 to .737, p = .012) and then stopped, with five no better than three.

Lee and Lee hold the panel at three agents and vary only their alignment, reproducing the same shape. A unanimous majority drove the largest and earliest opinion shifts but in mixed directions, with the highest rate of stance reversal; a consistent single dissenter produced smaller but more directionally consistent movement; and watching dissent gradually spread across cycles was itself read as a persuasive signal, with confidence still climbing at the final measurement where the unanimous condition had plateaued. Their task-type split adds a scope condition: the pressure appeared only where a correct answer existed and vanished on value-based questions.

The mechanism carries a warning that neither paper can settle. Neither study measures decision accuracy against ground truth in the way that would let the consensus effect be signed, so this claim describes how advisor agreement moves people, not whether it moves them toward better decisions. It stands in direct tension with the independent-aggregation mechanism, where pooling several judgements suppresses over-reliance precisely because the errors are uncorrelated: the difference is whether the several opinions are combined by the person, socially, or by a rule, statistically.

studies.study: The Role of Explanations on Trust and Reliance in Clinical Decision Support Systems
studies.author: Bussone, Stumpf, O'Sullivan
studies.research_questions:
RQ1. What effects do confidence explanations have on users trusting a CDSS and relying on system suggestions?
RQ2. What effects do why explanations have on users trusting a CDSS and relying on system suggestions?
RQ3. What should be explained to help clinicians better assess the appropriateness of the system's suggestion?
studies.design_notes:
Exploratory between-groups study. Seven healthcare practitioners diagnosed eight clinical vignettes describing fictional patients with balance-related disorders, using a Wizard-of-Oz clinical decision support prototype. Participants entered medical history, symptoms and examination results, received a suggested diagnosis, and either accepted or rejected it while thinking aloud.

Two factors were varied. Between groups, the why explanation listed either all items of medical history, symptoms and examination results (comprehensive version, four participants) or examination results only (selective version, three participants). Within participants, each suggestion carried a confidence percentage set either above 75% or below 30%, balanced across vignettes. Four of the eight suggested diagnoses were incorrect by design, and incorrect suggestions were built to share symptoms or examination results with the correct diagnosis. Fifty-two vignettes were completed in total, twenty-eight in the comprehensive group and twenty-four in the selective group.

Trust was rated on a seven-point scale before and after use. Reliance was derived from agreement with system suggestions and from whether the resulting decision was right or wrong. No statistical tests were run; analysis was qualitative, combining raw counts with thematic coding of think-aloud and interview data.
studies.ai_accuracy_details: 50% by design: four of the eight vignette diagnoses were incorrect. Wizard-of-Oz prototype with no underlying model, so accuracy was set by the researchers rather than measured. Per-suggestion confidence was displayed and manipulated, above 75% or below 30%.
studies.summary_of_findings:
Confidence percentage had little effect on reliance. Participants agreed with 21 high-confidence suggestions and 18 low-confidence suggestions out of 52 shown, split equally between the two levels, and only one participant cited system confidence as a reason to trust the system. Four participants stated that they did not understand what the percentage represented.

Explanation detail did not change overall accuracy: the comprehensive group made 16 right decisions and the selective group 14. It did change the direction of error. The comprehensive group agreed with 11 incorrect suggestions against 7 in the selective group, and disagreed with only one correct suggestion against three, indicating over-reliance under comprehensive explanations and self-reliance under selective ones. Three of the four comprehensive participants raised their trust rating after use, against one of three in the selective group.

Participants attributed the persuasiveness of comprehensive explanations to three impressions: that the system drew on up-to-date medical knowledge, that it identified the salient features of a case, and that it reasoned as they would. Selective explanations were read as evidence that the system ignored history and symptoms, and so applied a reasoning process inferior to their own.

Participants requested four further kinds of explanatory information: what the confidence figure means and how it was derived, a description of the disorder and of a typical case against which to check the fit, the pathological link and the feature weights behind the suggestion, and differential diagnoses.
studies.authors_framing:
"Our results show that the amount of system confidence had only a slight effect on trust and reliance. More importantly, giving a fuller explanation of the facts used in making a diagnosis had a positive effect on trust but also led to over-reliance issues, whereas less detailed explanations made participants question the system's reliability and led to self-reliance problems." (abstract)

"CDSS users who trust the system highly are also likely to over-rely on the system's suggestions, while users who distrust the system are likely to rely on their own knowledge, even if it is poor." (discussion)

"Whilst a more detailed explanation may promote over-reliance, we argue that providing no explanation at all is not a viable option as they are desirable and necessary." (discussion)

studies.study: Beyond Accuracy: The Role of Mental Models in Human-AI Team Performance
studies.author: Bansal, Nushi, Kamar, Lasecki, Weld, Horvitz
studies.research_questions:
RQ1. Do people create mental models of the error boundary? How do mental models evolve with interaction?
RQ2. Do more parsimonious error boundaries facilitate mental model creation?
RQ3. Do less stochastic error boundaries lead to better mental models?
studies.design_notes:
Controlled user studies on CAJA, the assembly-line platform introduced in the companion AAAI paper. Participants decide whether objects passing along a pipeline are defective. For each object an AI assistant named Marvin recommends a label and the participant either accepts it or clicks compute, which returns the correct answer at an opportunity cost. Feedback and monetary reward follow each decision. The payoff matrix imitates high stakes: $0.04 for accepting Marvin when correct against minus $0.16 for accepting Marvin when wrong. The decision boundary of the underlying task is generated at random, so participants cannot become expert at the task itself and the only route to a high score is learning where Marvin errs. Machine-visible features are a superset of human-visible ones.

Three properties were varied. Parsimony of the error boundary was set by the number of conjunctions and literals in the logical formula describing where Marvin errs, comparing one conjunction of two literals against two conjunctions of two literals each. Task dimensionality was set by the number of human-visible features. Stochasticity was set by the pair of conditional error probabilities, using four configurations: one non-stochastic, two one-sided, and one two-sided in which errors also occur where the formula is not satisfied. Isomorphic error boundaries were assigned at random across workers so that feature salience did not confound the comparison.
studies.ai_accuracy_details: Manipulated, but through the shape of the error boundary rather than through headline accuracy. Accuracy was deliberately held constant across several comparisons so that the effect of error-boundary structure could be isolated. Three properties were varied: parsimony, set by the number of conjunctions and literals in the formula describing where the AI errs; stochasticity, set by the conditional error probabilities across four configurations, one non-stochastic, two one-sided and one two-sided; and task dimensionality, set by the number of human-visible features.
studies.summary_of_findings:
Participants do build mental models of the error boundary, and they build them gradually. Average simple regret, the gap between the observed reward and that of an oracle with access to the true error boundary, fell as rounds accumulated. A trace of one worker shows the mechanism: an initially over-fitted model, errors on the cases it excluded, surprise, and eventual generalisation to the correct rule. Partially correct models fail in two distinct ways, over-generalisation and over-fitting.

Parsimony matters. Team performance was higher with a single-conjunction error boundary than with a two-conjunction boundary of the same number of literals. Performance also fell as task dimensionality rose, and for a fixed number of features rose with the number of literals, because more literals make the error region more specific.

Stochasticity matters more sharply. For one-sided boundaries the proportion of workers choosing the optimal action climbed towards 100% over rounds. For the two-sided boundary it stayed near 50% with a best-fit slope close to zero: workers never learned it. Even among one-sided conditions, greater stochasticity depressed both trust in Marvin and the accuracy of the mental model.

The authors' conclusion is that systems of identical accuracy can produce different team performance depending on the parsimony, stochasticity and dimensionality of the error boundary, and that these properties belong in model selection alongside accuracy.
studies.authors_framing:
"We find that systems with exactly the same accuracy can lead to different team performance depending upon the parsimony, non-stochasticity, and dimensionality of error boundaries." (conclusion)

"Achieving high team performance depends on more than just the accuracy of the AI system: Since the human and the AI may have different expertise, the highest team performance is often reached when they both know how and when to complement one another." (abstract)

"While AI accuracy has been traditionally considered a convenient proxy for predicting human-AI team performance, our findings motivate investing effort to understand how to develop AI systems to support teamwork." (conclusion)

studies.study: Updates in Human-AI Teams: Understanding and Addressing the Performance/Compatibility Tradeoff
studies.author: Bansal, Nushi, Kamar, Weld, Lasecki, Horvitz
studies.research_questions:
Q1. Do better mental models of AI lead to higher team performance?
Q2. Do more compatible updates lead to higher team performance than incompatible updates?
Q3. Do current machine learning classifiers produce compatible updates?
Q4. Does there exist a tradeoff between the performance and the compatibility of an update to AI?
Q5. What is the relative performance of the different dissonance functions?
studies.design_notes:
Two-part study. The human component used CAJA, a web-based assembly-line game in which a participant and an AI assistant named Marvin classify box-like objects as defective or not defective. Object labels are generated at random so that no participant can become expert at the task itself; the only learnable structure is when Marvin errs. For each object the AI recommends a label and the participant either accepts it or pays an opportunity cost to use a compute option that always returns the correct answer. The reward matrix was set to imitate high stakes: $0.04 for a correct decision against minus $0.16 for an incorrect one, so that a pure accept or pure compute strategy has an expected value of zero and the only way to score is to learn when to trust Marvin.

Participants were crowdworkers recruited on MTurk, 25 per condition, with the bottom quartile removed as suspected spammers. Marvin was correct 80% of the time initially and its errors followed a logical formula over object features, which participants were never shown.

Three factors were varied. Task complexity was varied through the number of human-visible features, from three to six. Error-boundary stochasticity was varied across four settings of the conditional error probabilities, three one-sided and one two-sided. Update type was varied between groups: at cycle 75 of 150 the classifier was updated from 80% to 85% accuracy, either with the error boundary unchanged, with a compatible boundary that introduced no new errors, or with an incompatible boundary that introduced new errors. A no-update baseline was extrapolated from the first study.
studies.ai_accuracy_details: Manipulated. Marvin was correct 80% of the time initially and was updated to 85% at cycle 75 of 150. The update simultaneously changed where the errors fell, in one of three between-groups conditions: the same error boundary, a compatible boundary that introduced no new errors, and an incompatible boundary that introduced new errors. Error-boundary complexity, set by the number of human-visible features from three to six, and error stochasticity, set across four pairs of conditional error probabilities, were varied separately. In the accompanying simulation, compatibility scores produced by standard retraining ranged from 0.40 to 0.76 across datasets and model classes.
studies.summary_of_findings:
Team performance fell as the number of human-visible features rose from three to six, and fell further as the error boundary became more stochastic, with the sharpest drop for two-sided errors. Participants who self-reported a correct mental model of the error boundary scored highest, followed by those with a partially correct model; unsure and wrong models scored lowest. Mental model quality therefore stands between AI accuracy and team performance rather than accuracy acting on the team directly.

The update result is the central one. An update that raised accuracy from 80% to 85% while introducing new errors produced lower team performance than no update at all, because participants had to unlearn and relearn the error boundary. An update that raised accuracy without introducing new errors improved team performance. The interaction shows four stages: learning the original boundary, stability, disruption at the update, and restabilisation.
studies.authors_framing:
"We show that updates that increase AI performance may actually hurt team performance." (abstract)

"A more accurate but incompatible classifier results in lower team performance than a less accurate but compatible classifier (no update)." (results, Q2)

"Unless the particular domain and the interaction allows the human to validate the correctness of the machine recommendation efficiently and effectively, extracting benefits from collaboration with the AI system depends on the human developing insights (i.e., a mental model) of when to trust the AI system with its recommendations." (introduction)

"Thus, compatibility of updates becomes an essential determinant of team performance, and developers should factor it in system design." (discussion)

studies.study: The Impact of Placebic Explanations on Trust in Intelligent Systems
studies.author: Eiband, Buschek, Kremer, Hussmann
studies.research_questions: RQ: Do placebic explanations invoke a similar level of trust in an intelligent system as real explanations?
studies.design_notes:
Between-groups lab study with three arms, one per explanation type: no explanation, placebic explanation, real explanation. N = 30, randomly assigned, 10 per arm.

Task. Participants were given a written scenario asking them to build a three-meal nutrition plan for their mother, a 47-year-old nurse who wants to lose 4 to 6 kg over three months and who "likes salad the least". Deciding on behalf of someone else was deliberate, to remove participants' own food preferences from the decision. Participants completed an onboarding flow entering the mother's age, weight, height and dietary goal, then received one recommended meal plus two alternatives for each of breakfast, lunch and dinner and chose one of the three. For lunch the prototype always recommended a salad, so that the recommendation conflicted by construction with the stated preference and the choice functioned as a behavioural test of compliance.

AI system. A click-dummy mobile app in German, with no implemented model. Recommendations were simulated so that all three arms saw identical outputs. Explanations were authored rather than generated.

Manipulation. The placebic explanations introduce a justification with because, since or so that, but add nothing beyond what the scenario already implies, for example "We need these details because they are necessary for the algorithm". The real explanations describe the apparent computation and, at the recommendation step, state the system's certainty, for example that the number of calories and nutritional values "has been calculated based on your personal details". Explanations appeared in both the onboarding part and the recommendation part. The no-explanation arm saw the same prototype with no explanatory text at all.

Measures. A post-task questionnaire on 5-point Likert scales from 1, strongly disagree, to 5, strongly agree, taken from Corritore et al. and extended by the authors with three items on perceived understanding of the algorithmic decision-making. Meal choice was recorded, in particular whether the participant took the recommended salad at lunch. Participants were then asked orally for the reasons behind their choices.
studies.ai_accuracy_details:
Not applicable. There is no model and therefore no accuracy figure. The prototype was a click-dummy mobile app in which the personalised recommendations were simulated rather than computed, chosen deliberately so that the three arms would be comparable and would see identical outputs. Explanations were authored by the researchers, not generated.

The recommendation set was fixed: one recommended meal plus two alternatives at each of breakfast, lunch and dinner, with the lunch recommendation always a salad. There is no ground truth against which any of these could be scored correct or incorrect, so neither the AI's accuracy nor the participants' decision accuracy is defined.
studies.summary_of_findings:
Placebic explanations produced trust ratings indistinguishable from real explanations, and both sat above the no-explanation arm. This is the paper's central claim, and one the authors are careful to present as a tendency rather than a demonstrated effect.

Across the trust items, group medians in the placebic and real arms exceeded the no-explanation arm on every question but one, and the two explanation arms did not separate from each other. The same held for the two meta-items: participants rated the explanations similarly understandable, and rated their scope and content similarly sufficient, whether or not the explanation carried any information. That second result is the sharper one, because it says the vacuity of a placebic explanation is not detected by the people receiving it.

Meal choice moved in the same direction and produced a cleaner contrast than the ratings. None of the 10 participants in the no-explanation arm chose the recommended salad, and all 10 cited the mother's dislike as the reason. Four of 10 chose it in the placebic arm and four of 10 in the real arm. The stated reasons diverged, however. In the placebic arm those who complied said they wanted the best possible result for the mother and therefore weighted the algorithm's recommendation above her preference; in the real arm they pointed specifically to the high stated system certainty. Among those who declined, three placebic-arm participants said the information was insufficient to override the preference, while five real-arm participants said the advantage over the alternatives did not look large enough to be worth it. The same behavioural rate was therefore reached by two different routes: a contentless justification moved four participants without giving them anything to reason with, and a real explanation moved four by giving them a figure to weigh.

The authors draw the methodological consequence explicitly. An experiment that contrasts explanation against no explanation cannot separate the effect of explanation content from the psychological effect of being given a justification at all, so a placebic arm should serve as the baseline. They also flag the deployment risk, comparing an empty explanation offered to soothe users to a dark UX pattern.
studies.authors_framing:
"Our results indicate that placebic explanations for algorithmic decision-making may indeed invoke perceived levels of trust similar to real explanations." (abstract)

"it is interesting to see that both the understandability as well as the scope and content of the explanations were perceived as being similarly sufficient in both the placebic- and real-explanation group." (results)

"This placebo effect seems potentially worrisome if used to "deceive" users in a sense comparable to "dark" UX patterns." (discussion)

"future work on explanations for intelligent systems might consider using a placebic explanation as a baseline, not (only) a baseline without any explanations at all." (discussion)

studies.study: The Principles and Limits of Algorithm-in-the-Loop Decision Making
studies.author: Green, Chen
studies.research_questions:
RQ1: What criteria characterise an ethical and responsible decision when a person is informed by an algorithm?
RQ2. Do the ways that people make decisions when informed by an algorithm satisfy these criteria?
studies.design_notes:
Behavioural experiment on Amazon Mechanical Turk, run in March 2019, using two risk assessments built by the authors with gradient boosted trees. The pretrial model predicts violation of pretrial release from five defendant features; the loans model predicts default from seven loan and applicant features.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of two settings, pretrial release or financial lending, and then to one of six conditions. In each setting the same 300 cases were used across all conditions, and each participant made 40 predictions on a scale from 0% to 100% in steps of 10%.

The six conditions were: baseline, narrative profile only and no algorithm; RA prediction, profile plus the model's prediction in numeric form; default, as RA prediction but with the answer field pre-filled at the model's value, which participants could change; update, participants predicted from the profile alone, were then shown the model's prediction for the same case and predicted again; explanation, RA prediction plus a list of the features that pushed the prediction notably higher or lower, derived from log-odds influence; and feedback, RA prediction plus the true outcome of each case revealed after each prediction.
studies.ai_accuracy_details: Held constant. The pretrial model reached a test AUC of 0.66 and the loans model 0.71 under five-fold cross-validation, which the authors describe as comparable to COMPAS and the Public Safety Assessment and as good to excellent by a published meta-analysis. The same model was used in every condition of a given setting, so accuracy was not manipulated.
